target.title: God and the View From Nowhere: De Se Knowledge and Divine Omniscience
target.thesis: Given libertarian freedom and robust moral responsibility, divine omniscience must include irreducible self-locating knowledge.

argument.title: Self-Location Constraint

atoms.A: an agent is robustly contrastively responsible for bringing about one outcome rather than alternatives
atoms.B: the agent's cognition represents the outcome as issuing from its own action or activity
atoms.C: divine cognition represents God as the source of actualising W1 rather than W0
atoms.D: a third-personal proposition identifies God as actualising a world
atoms.E: a proposition represents that actualisation under the first-personal aspect required for source attribution
atoms.F: God is robustly contrastively responsible for actualising W1 rather than W0
atoms.G: God is contrastively responsible for actualising one world rather than another
atoms.H: divine cognition includes irreducible de se content

argument.missing_premise: God's contrastive responsibility for actualising one world rather than another is robust responsibility, and representing God as the source of that actualisation requires irreducible de se content. [(G -> F) & (C -> H)]

W7203485685.c001.text: On the Thomistic model, divine cognition is identical with the divine essence and divine being.
W7203485685.c001.quote: On the Thomistic model, divine cognition is neither discursive nor representational, but identical with the divine essence itself. God knows God through a single timeless act identical with God’s being

W7203485685.c002.text: Classical theists often hold that divine cognition is wholly non-indexical and lacks essentially first-personal or self-locating structure.
W7203485685.c002.quote: Classical theists accordingly often understand divine cognition as wholly non-indexical. On this view, God does not know God by occupying a cognitive standpoint distinct from what is known.

W7203485685.c003.text: Strictly non-indexical accounts of divine cognition may be unable to explain libertarian and morally responsible divine agency.
W7203485685.c003.quote: Taken together, these discussions raise the question whether strictly non-indexical accounts of divine cognition can adequately explain libertarian and morally responsible divine agency.

W7203485685.c004.text: An agent is robustly responsible for an action only if the agent can be identified as its source rather than the source of relevant alternatives.
W7203485685.c004.quote: I adopt a robust contrastive conception of responsibility according to which an agent is responsible for φ only if the agent can be identified as the source of φ rather than relevant alternatives.

W7203485685.c005.text: If an agent is robustly responsible for bringing about one outcome rather than another, its cognition must represent the first outcome as its own action.
W7203485685.c005.quote: If an agent is robustly responsible for bringing about φ rather than ψ, then the agent’s cognitive state must represent φ as the outcome of its own action rather than ψ.

W7203485685.c006.text: Robust contrastive responsibility requires cognition that represents an outcome as issuing from the agent's own activity rather than relevant alternatives.
W7203485685.c006.quote: where responsibility is understood contrastively, the cognitive state constitutive of responsible agency must itself represent the relevant outcome as issuing from the agent’s own activity rather than the relevant alternatives.

W7203485685.c007.text: Self-ascriptive cognition is constitutive of robust contrastive agency attribution, rather than merely a practical aid for finite agents.
W7203485685.c007.quote: Rather, de se cognition is constitutive of robust contrastive agency attribution itself.

W7203485685.c008.text: A third-personal proposition identifying God as actualising a world does not itself represent that actualisation under the first-personal aspect required for source attribution.
W7203485685.c008.quote: A third-personal proposition such as “God actualises W1” may identify the correct agent extensionally, yet it does not by itself represent the actualisation under the first-personal aspect required for source attribution.

W7203485685.c009.text: If God is robustly responsible for actualising one world rather than another, divine cognition must include self-locating content representing God as its source.
W7203485685.c009.quote: If God is robustly responsible for actualising one world rather than another, then divine cognition must include self-locating content representing God as the source of that actualisation.

W7203485685.c010.text: Strong non-indexical models of omniscience exclude irreducibly de se content.
W7203485685.c010.quote: Strong non-indexical models of omniscience exclude irreducibly de se content.

W7203485685.c011.text: Strong non-indexical models of omniscience cannot account for robust contrastive divine responsibility.
W7203485685.c011.quote: Therefore, strong non-indexical models of omniscience cannot account for robust contrastive divine responsibility.

W7203485685.c012.text: The argument is conditional on libertarian agency and robust contrastive responsibility.
W7203485685.c012.quote: The argument is conditional. Those who reject libertarian agency or robust contrastive responsibility may reject premise (1).

W7203485685.c013.text: On a strong non-indexical interpretation of omniscience, divine cognition contains no irreducible de se structure.
W7203485685.c013.quote: The present argument targets a stronger non-indexical reading according to which divine cognition contains no irreducible de se structure whatsoever.

W7203485685.c014.text: Classical divine simplicity holds that divine omniscience, omnipotence, goodness, and being are numerically identical with the divine essence.
W7203485685.c014.quote: On stronger formulations of simplicity, divine omniscience, omnipotence, goodness, and being are all numerically identical with the divine essence.

W7203485685.c015.text: Strictly non-indexical divine cognition lacks irreducibly first-personal or self-locating structure.
W7203485685.c015.quote: Since the act, object, and subject of divine knowledge are identical, divine self-knowledge contains no irreducibly first-personal or self-locating structure.

W7203485685.c016.text: A strictly non-indexical divine cognition is difficult to reconcile with robustly contrastive divine agency.
W7203485685.c016.quote: The difficulty, however, is that a strictly non-indexical conception of divine cognition appears difficult to reconcile with robustly contrastive divine agency.

W7203485685.c017.text: If divine will is necessary and identical with divine essence, the contingency of creation is difficult to explain.
W7203485685.c017.quote: If the divine will is necessary and identical with the divine essence, then the contingency of creation becomes difficult to explain.

W7203485685.c018.text: Can strictly non-indexical omniscience account for divine responsibility for actualising one world rather than another?
W7203485685.c018.quote: The central question is whether such a conception of omniscience can account for divine responsibility for actualising one world rather than another.

W7203485685.c019.text: No adequately developed account currently shows how irreducible de se content can occur in a single timeless, simple divine act without metaphysical composition.
W7203485685.c019.quote: The present claim is only that no adequately developed account of this kind is presently available.

W7203485685.c020.text: If such an account is provided, divine simplicity need not be rejected, but divine omniscience cannot remain strictly non-indexical.
W7203485685.c020.quote: If such an account can be provided, then the conclusion is not that simplicity should be rejected, but that divine omniscience cannot remain strictly non-indexical.

W7203485685.c021.text: Indexicals convey information about a subject's cognitive position within a representational context.
W7203485685.c021.quote: Indexical expressions therefore contain information about the cognitive position of a subject within a context of representation.

W7203485685.c022.text: Some self-locating knowledge cannot be reduced to de dicto or de re representation.
W7203485685.c022.quote: Perry (1979) and Lewis (1979) argue that certain forms of self-locating knowledge cannot be reduced to de dicto or de re representation.

W7203485685.c023.text: A complete specification of third-personal facts can fail to determine the cognitive state required for agency.
W7203485685.c023.quote: A complete specification of third-personal facts may therefore fail to determine the cognitive state required for agency.

W7203485685.c024.text: Purely third-personal representation is insufficient to explain agency under robust contrastive responsibility.
W7203485685.c024.quote: Under these conditions, purely third-personal representation appears insufficient for explaining agency.

W7203485685.c025.text: Given libertarian agency and robust contrastive responsibility, purely uncentred divine knowledge is insufficient for agency-sensitive explanation.
W7203485685.c025.quote: The remainder of the paper argues that, given libertarian agency and robust contrastive responsibility, it is not.

W7203485685.c026.text: Libertarian agency and robust contrastive responsibility require an explanation of why an agent actualises one possible world rather than relevant alternatives.
W7203485685.c026.quote: If robust contrastive responsibility requires explanation of why this outcome is attributable to this agent rather than relevant alternatives, then de se content appears indispensable.

W7203485685.c027.text: Third-personal truths about God actualising a world do not determine the self-ascriptive content required for robust contrastive responsibility.
W7203485685.c027.quote: Third-personal truths therefore underdetermine the de se content required for robust contrastive responsibility.

W7203485685.c028.text: Knowing that God actualises W1 is not equivalent in action-guiding contexts to representing oneself as the source of actualising W1 rather than W0.
W7203485685.c028.quote: Knowing that God actualises W1 is not equivalent, in action-guiding contexts, to representing oneself as the source of actualising W1 rather than W0.

W7203485685.c029.text: Actualisation creates an explanatory asymmetry between an actualised world and merely possible alternatives, even on timeless models of divine knowledge.
W7203485685.c029.quote: Even on timeless models of divine knowledge, actualisation introduces an explanatory asymmetry between W1 and relevant alternatives.

W7203485685.c030.text: The Self-Location Constraint concerns source attribution by agency rather than God's spatiotemporal location or presence.
W7203485685.c030.quote: The issue is not temporal sequence but source attribution.

W7203485685.c031.text: Robust contrastive responsibility requires divine cognition to represent God as the source of actualising W1 rather than W0.
W7203485685.c031.quote: The relevant question is not merely which world becomes actual, but whether divine cognition represents God as the source of actualising W1 rather than W0.

W7203485685.c032.text: A de se state fixes the agent as the source of an outcome, whereas a third-personal state may remain merely recognitional.
W7203485685.c032.quote: By contrast, the de se state “I actualise W1 rather than W0” fixes the agent as the source of the relevant outcome.

W7203485685.c033.text: Strictly non-indexical omniscience is insufficient to explain libertarian, robustly contrastively responsible divine agency.
W7203485685.c033.quote: The central claim is that non-indexical omniscience, understood as exhaustive knowledge of all true uncentred propositions, is insufficient for explaining libertarian and contrastively responsible divine agency.

W7203485685.c034.text: Extensional equivalence between third-personal and first-personal propositions does not preserve their explanatory role in responsible agency.
W7203485685.c034.quote: Substitution of co-referring expressions may preserve truth while altering explanatory role.

W7203485685.c035.text: The Self-Location Constraint requires cognition to represent both the outcome that obtains and the subject as its source.
W7203485685.c035.quote: A cognitive state satisfies SLC only if it represents both which outcome obtains and the subject as the source of that outcome.

W7203485685.c036.text: The Self-Location Constraint applies only when genuine modal alternatives exist and libertarian agency generates a contrastive explanatory demand.
W7203485685.c036.quote: The Self-Location Constraint therefore applies only where libertarian agency and robust contrastive responsibility generate an explanatory requirement to account for why one possible world is actualised rather than another.

W7203485685.c037.text: Divine simplicity prohibits metaphysical composition but may permit intentional complexity and irreducible de se content.

W7203485685.c038.text: The argument does not establish that divine simplicity conflicts with de se cognition; it targets only wholly non-indexical omniscience.
W7203485685.c038.quote: It establishes only that strict non-indexicality is insufficient.

W7203485685.c039.text: Defenders of classical theism may contend that a single timeless, simple divine cognition includes irreducible de se content without metaphysical composition.
W7203485685.c039.quote: Likewise, defenders of classical theism may argue that a single timeless and simple act of cognition can include irreducible de se content without introducing metaphysical composition.

W7203485685.c040.text: Because there is exactly one divine agent, third-personal knowledge that God actualises W1 rather than W0 plus knowledge that I am God suffices for de se knowledge.
W7203485685.c040.quote: Since there is exactly one divine agent, knowledge that “God actualises W1 rather than W0”, together with knowledge of the identity “I = God”, appears sufficient to yield the content “I actualise W1 rather than W0.”

W7203485685.c041.text: Extensional equivalence between third-personal and de se contents does not establish their explanatory equivalence for agency.
W7203485685.c041.quote: This objection, however, conflates extensional equivalence with explanatory equivalence.

W7203485685.c042.text: Self-locating cognition has an action-guiding explanatory role that is not exhausted by third-personal representation.
W7203485685.c042.quote: The central claim of the de se literature is not merely that indexical expressions behave differently in language, but that self-locating cognition performs an explanatory role not exhausted by third-personal representation.

W7203485685.c043.text: Knowledge that God actualises W1 rather than W0 identifies the outcome but does not represent actualisation as issuing from God’s own agency.
W7203485685.c043.quote: Knowledge that “God actualises W1 rather than W0” specifies which contrastive outcome obtains, but does not yet represent divine agency under the aspect required for contrastive explanation.

W7203485685.c044.text: Robust contrastive responsibility requires cognition that explains why an outcome is attributable to an agent rather than relevant alternatives.
W7203485685.c044.quote: It requires cognition capable of explaining why this outcome is attributable to this agent rather than relevant alternatives.

W7203485685.c045.text: God’s knowledge of the actual world through causing it may seem to supply the cognition required for contrastive agency explanation.
W7203485685.c045.quote: A related objection appeals to divine knowledge-by-causation. God knows the actual world because God causes it.

W7203485685.c046.text: A causal relation between divine agency and actuality does not itself establish self-ascriptive cognition adequate for contrastive agency explanation.
W7203485685.c046.quote: Knowing by causing may establish a metaphysical relation between divine agency and actuality while leaving open whether divine cognition includes the self-ascriptive representation required for contrastive agency explanation.

W7203485685.c047.text: Exhaustive third-personal cognition alone is insufficient for the explanatory demands of robust contrastive responsibility.
W7203485685.c047.quote: It does not show that exhaustive third-personal cognition is sufficient for the explanatory demands imposed by robust contrastive responsibility.

W7203485685.c048.text: Divine simplicity need not preclude internally differentiated explanatory structure, because one timeless cognitive act can have distinct explanatory aspects without metaphysical parts.
W7203485685.c048.quote: A single timeless act of cognition may admit distinct explanatory aspects without thereby consisting of metaphysical parts.

W7203485685.c049.text: A semantically stratified divine cognition could preserve simplicity while including de se representation needed to explain divine agency contrastively.
W7203485685.c049.quote: Divine cognition remains simple and timeless while including the self-ascriptive structure required for representing divine agency as the source of actuality.

W7203485685.c050.text: Necessitarianism avoids the SLC by denying genuine divine alternatives and thus rejecting the conditions for robust contrastive responsibility.
W7203485685.c050.quote: Necessitarianism resolves that tension not by incorporating de se cognition into omniscience, but by denying the modal conditions under which robust contrastive responsibility arises.

W7203485685.c051.text: Strong non-indexical omniscience, libertarian divine agency, and robust contrastive responsibility cannot all be maintained together.
W7203485685.c051.quote:
What cannot be simultaneously maintained, however, is:
 
●
strong non-indexical omniscience;
 
●
libertarian divine agency;
 
●
robust contrastive responsibility.

W7203485685.c052.text: If God is contrastively responsible for actualising one world rather than another, divine cognition must include irreducible de se content.
W7203485685.c052.quote: If God is responsible for actualising one world rather than another, divine cognition must include irreducible de se content representing actuality as issuing from divine agency.

W7203485685.c053.text: Whether a single timeless and simple divine act of cognition can include self-locating content remains the central question.
W7203485685.c053.quote: The central question, therefore, is not whether omniscience is possible, but whether a single timeless and simple act of cognition can include self-locating content.

W7203485685.arg1.mp.text: God's contrastive responsibility for actualising one world rather than another is robust responsibility, and representing God as the source of that actualisation requires irreducible de se content.

W7203485685.a1.text: Purely non-indexical models of divine omniscience cannot explain libertarian, morally responsible divine agency.
W7203485685.a1.quote: I argue that classical non-indexical models of divine omniscience are insufficient to account for divine agency conceived as both libertarian and morally responsible.

W7203485685.a2.text: An omniscient agent with robust contrastive responsibility must know de se that it actualizes this world rather than alternatives.
W7203485685.a2.quote: an omniscient agent capable of robust contrastive responsibility must not only know all truths, but also know de se that it is the agent actualising a particular world rather than relevant alternatives.

W7203485685.a3.text: Theism requires self-locating omniscience if libertarianism and robust contrastive responsibility are true.
W7203485685.a3.quote: I conclude that, given libertarianism and robust contrastive responsibility, theism requires a form of omniscience that includes self-locating knowledge.

W7203485685.arg1.r1.text: Robust contrastive responsibility requires that the agent's cognition represent the outcome under an agent-relative aspect (a stance of doing, not merely knowing) that a rigid third-personal identifier cannot supply.

W7203485685.arg1.r2.text: Robust contrastive responsibility requires cognition that represents the selected outcome, under the contrast with its alternative, as the result of an act the cognizing agent herself performs and intends, not merely as a state of the world tied to an impersonal lever-state.

W7203485685.arg1.r3.text: Robust contrastive responsibility requires that the agent's cognition represent the selected outcome, under its contrast with the alternative, as the result of an act the agent herself performs and intends, rather than representing the outcome itself as her action.

W7203485685.arg1.r4.text: Robust contrastive responsibility requires that the agent's cognition represent the selected outcome, under the contrast with its alternative, as the result of an act the cognizing agent herself performs and intends, not merely as a state tied to a value-indexed structure.

objections.text: Consider a long-running coastal engineer, Mara, who sets a sea wall's height by a stored model of tides. Her cognition does not represent herself as 'the source' of the wall's height; it represents the wall at 4 metres as the output of a calculation that fixes the tide threshold, and she can say which alternative heights she rejected and why. Suppose the town later asks who is responsible for the wall being 4 metres rather than 3. Mara is robustly contrastively responsible: had she chosen 3, the flood would have come, and her choice is the difference-maker. Yet her cognition contains no first-personal marker that the height issues from her agency. It contains the content 'the wall is 4 m because the threshold is 4 m,' with her choice modelled as one causal node among others. Her responsibility is secured by counterfactual dependence and by the structure of her deliberation over relevant alternatives, not by any self-representation of the outcome as her own. The same structure can hold for an agent whose cognition is wholly third-personal about the outcome while representing its contrastive alternatives explicitly.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise c031 fails because it requires divine cognition to represent God as the source of W1 rather than W0, yet Mara's case shows robust contrastive responsibility can be secured by cognition that represents the outcome and its rejected alternatives without any source-representing, first-personal content.

objections.text: Ines, a reservoir controller, faces rising water during a storm. Opening the east spillway will flood farmland; doing nothing will let the dam overtop and flood the town. She studies hydrographs, weighs crop losses against lives, and concludes, in exactly these terms, 'The farmland should flood rather than the town.' She opens the spillway and the farmland floods. The inquiry finds her robustly responsible for the farmland flooding rather than the town: she foresaw it, compared it with the alternative, chose it knowingly, and could have done otherwise. Yet the outcome she represented, the farmland under water, was never represented as her action. It is a hydrological event downstream, and she represented it as one. The only thing she represented as her doing was turning the spillway wheel, and that is a different item from the outcome for which she is held responsible. Her responsibility for the flood rests on representing the flood as a foreseen consequence she was choosing between, not on representing the flood as her action.
objections.premise_fails_because: W7203485685.c005 fails because Ines is robustly responsible for the farmland flooding rather than the town while her cognition represents that outcome only as a foreseen consequence she chose, not as her own action.

objections.text: A control-room operator, Mira, selects lever A after reviewing two labeled simulations: A will divert a flood into an empty quarry; B will divert it into a village. She intends to save the village and pulls A. Her display represents only impersonal propositions: “A opens gate 1,” “gate 1 sends water to quarry,” and “B sends water to village.” It never represents the flood outcome as issuing from Mira’s own activity; it tracks lever states and consequences. The gate opens, the flood reaches the quarry, and the village is saved. Mira is robustly contrastively responsible for the quarry outcome rather than the village outcome: she knew the alternatives, deliberately selected the difference-making option, and would have pulled B had she intended the village outcome. Yet her cognition need not represent the outcome as issuing from her own activity rather than the alternative.
objections.premise_fails_because: W7203485685.c006 fails because robust contrastive responsibility can arise from deliberate, informed selection among alternatives even when cognition represents only impersonal causal relations.

objections.text: God’s cognition uses only a rigid identifier, “G,” for the unique being whose intentions directly control which world becomes actual. G considers W0 and W1, judges W1 better, forms the intention expressed as “G will actualise W1,” and W1 consequently becomes actual. G then knows the proposition “G actualised W1 rather than W0 because G intended W1.” The identifier is third-personal: it carries no first-personal mode of presentation. Yet the proposition identifies the source perfectly. It singles out the unique controller, connects that being’s intention to the resulting world, and excludes every alternative source. Nothing further supplied by “I actualised W1” would improve the attribution of the actualisation to G.
objections.premise_fails_because: W7203485685.c008 fails because a third-personal proposition can identify God’s intention and controlling activity as the source of actualisation without representing them under a first-personal aspect.

objections.text: Consider a divine cognition that represents the proposition 'God actualises W1' and, in addition, represents W1 as preferred over W0 by a standard it itself instantiates, with no de se indexical content. Call it a purely third-personal but evaluatively structured representation. Now suppose a second agent, an idealised engineer modelled on this God, whose cognition likewise contains the indexical-free content 'the agent with goodness G selects W1 over W0 because G favours W1.' The engineer is robustly and contrastively responsible for selecting W1 rather than W0: the selection flows from her own values, would have differed had her values differed, and no alternative source intervenes. Yet her cognition contains no first-personal 'I am the source' representation. The premise assumes that robust contrastive responsibility requires self-representation as source, but the case shows that source-tracking can be carried by a counterfactually sensitive, value-indexed structure that the agent's own cognition encodes without irreducible de se content. The inference from robust responsibility to irreducible de se content therefore lacks support.
objections.premise_fails_because: The premise wrongly assumes that representing God as source of W1 over W0 requires irreducible de se content, when counterfactually sensitive, value-indexed third-personal representation can secure robust contrastive source-attribution without it.

objections.text: God creates an initial state containing two free creatures, Ada and Ben. Whether Ada will later betray Ben is genuinely unsettled. Nothing in God's decree, nature, or knowledge fixes it, because no fact about it exists yet. Let W1 be the history where Ada betrays and W0 the history where she stays loyal. They share every divine act and differ only in Ada's choice. God is robustly responsible for creating this risky, open arrangement rather than a closed or empty one. God weighed the stakes, knew betrayal was possible, and accepted that risk for the sake of real love. Yet divine cognition cannot represent God as the source of W1 rather than W0. At creation there is no settled W1 to represent, and once Ada chooses, she is the source of that contrast, not God. God's robust responsibility attaches to the contrast between opening this field of possibilities and not opening it. It does not attach to the complete-world contrast, so it never needs the representation c031 demands.
objections.premise_fails_because: W7203485685.c031 fails because in an open future God is robustly responsible for creating an unsettled world without being, or representing himself as, the source of one complete world rather than another.

objections.text: Molinism holds that God knows, before creating, every true counterfactual of creaturely freedom. God knows that if placed in circumstances C, Mara would freely help, while if placed in D, she would freely refuse. God considers W1, containing C, and W0, containing D, under complete third-personal descriptions: in W1 Mara helps; in W0 Mara refuses. God chooses to actualise W1 because its freely chosen goods are preferable. The choice is robustly contrastive: God could actualise W0, knows exactly its consequences, and intentionally actualises W1 instead. Yet the source attribution needed is exhausted by the true proposition that God actualises W1 rather than W0; no irreducible first-personal content is required. Divine responsibility arises from intentional selection among feasible worlds informed by middle knowledge, not from a de se mode of presentation.
objections.premise_fails_because: W7203485685.arg1.mp fails because Molinist divine responsibility for selecting W1 over W0 can rest on complete third-personal middle knowledge and intentional choice without irreducible de se content.

objections.text: Suppose God knows the third-personal truths that God alone intentionally actualises W1, that God could instead actualise W0, and that W1 occurs because of God’s fully informed, reason-responsive choice. God also has complete knowledge of every relevant alternative and causal dependency, but divine cognition contains no irreducible first-personal content. Nothing here prevents the choice from issuing from God, being controlled by God, or appropriately reflecting God’s reasons; omitting a distinct first-personal mode of presentation changes only how the source is represented, not who controls the outcome. Thus W7203485685.arg1.mp fails because source attribution can be fully represented by uniquely identifying third-personal content without irreducible de se content.
objections.premise_fails_because: Uniquely identifying third-personal cognition can attribute the actualisation to God as its controlled, intentional source without irreducible de se content.

objections.text: Consider Ada, a hydrologist who runs a dam control system by remote telemetry. She holds the rigid third-personal belief: 'the gate at Lock 9 is the one that floods the valley,' and she knows she is the one who issues the command that opens it. Her cognition contains no special 'stance of doing' term; she represents the outcome through a rigid description of the gate plus the plain fact that her keystrokes trigger it. Suppose she is contrastively responsible for flooding the valley rather than the eastern town: she chose Lock 9 over Lock 4 for reasons she can state in impersonal terms (elevation, soil saturation). Her representation of the flood is a third-personal proposition about Lock 9, yet she is robustly responsible, and nothing in her cognition is agent-relative beyond the causal fact that her input drives the gate. Agency is secured by causal control and contrastive reasons, not by an irreducible de se aspect. So the requirement that the agent's cognition carry an agent-relative stance a rigid identifier cannot supply is not necessary for robust contrastive responsibility.
objections.premise_fails_because: Premise r1 is false because Ada is robustly and contrastively responsible for flooding Lock 9's valley rather than the eastern town while her cognition represents the outcome only through a rigid third-personal identifier, showing that an agent-relative 'stance of doing' is not required.

objections.text: Consider a water-main control room. Engineer Ada holds a valve-state map: valve V open routes flow to district A, closed routes it to district B. She has no first-personal intention to 'do' this; her supervisor has ordered the switch, and a timer she set earlier fires automatically. Yet she knows exactly which outcome is hers under the contrast: she is the one who wired the timer and the flow goes to A because of her configuration. Her cognition represents the outcome contrastively as the result of the configured state she set up, not as an act she performs and intends at the moment of flow. Her responsibility for routing to A rather than B is robust: had she set the timer differently, the flow would have gone to B, and she would be blamed and credited accordingly. Her cognition contains no irreducible de se act-representation of the switching; it contains a third-personal state-description tied to her earlier decision. So robust contrastive responsibility does not require the agent's cognition to represent the selected outcome as the result of an act she herself performs and intends, in the present, under the contrast.
objections.premise_fails_because: The premise requires a present-tense, self-performed and intended act-representation for robust contrastive responsibility, but Ada's responsibility for routing to A rather than B is robust while her cognition represents the outcome only through a third-personal configured state she authored earlier.

objections.text: Consider Ada, a town clerk who must allot a single grant to either Riverside or Hillcrest. She reasons: 'Riverside has the better case, so the grant goes to Riverside.' Her cognition represents the outcome, Riverside funded, under its contrast with Hillcrest funded, and she intends it. Yet nothing in her thought represents the funding as the product of an act she herself performs. The content 'Riverside is funded because of the ranking' is entirely third-personal, and her responsibility for the allocation is nonetheless robust: had she ranked Hillcrest higher, Hillcrest would have been funded, and she would be blamed for either choice. Her cognition is intentionally directed at the contrast and at the outcome, with no first-personal self-representation as agent. So representing the selected outcome under its contrast, as the result of an intended act, is satisfiable without representing the outcome as one's own act. objections.text: Consider a water-network engineer, Ruth, who must choose between two valve configurations, C1 and C0, to route flow to a district. rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly challenges c008 as stated by claiming that a third-personal proposition can represent the actualisation with sufficient source attribution despite lacking a first-personal mode of presentation.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: The objection's G-proposition does pick out the unique controller and its intention, and I grant that it excludes rival sources. But the argument's demand, stated in c005 and c006, is not exclusion of other sources; it is that the cognition represent the outcome as issuing from the agent's own activity rather than from relevant alternatives. 'G actualised W1 rather than W0 because G intended W1' represents G as one bearer of a causal relation, which G can know without being in any position to take that relation as its own doing. The objection's own gloss, that the identifier 'carries no first-personal mode of presentation,' concedes the point at issue: the disputed content is precisely the mode of presentation. Note also that c030 holds the Self-Location Constraint concerns agency-based source attribution, not spatiotemporal presence, so the objection's appeal to a perfect identification is not yet an appeal to the right kind of attribution. A rigid designator fixes reference; it does not by itself fix the agent's stance toward the act. I would still press the objector to say why a third-personal representation of one's own intention and its effect should count as representing that effect as one's own action, since that is where the dispute now lies. The argument's bridge premise, that robust responsibility requires such agent-relative representation, remains the load-bearing and contestable step, and I would not claim the c008 rejoinder settles it.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: You distinguish identifying the agent from representing the act as “its own,” but you have not shown that the latter requires a first-personal mode of presentation. The G-proposition already represents the actualisation as issuing from G’s intention and activity, not merely as a causal relation borne by G. Since G is the cognizer, the proposition concerns the cognizer’s own intention and action even if it does not present them under “I.” Saying that G could know this without “taking” it as its own doing simply restates the disputed requirement. What responsibility-relevant difference would that further stance make? The representation already tracks who controlled the alternatives, which intention selected W1, and whose activity produced it. Unless robust responsibility depends on a special phenomenology or practical role available only to first-personal content, your appeal to “own activity” cannot establish c008; it merely builds irreducible de se representation into that phrase.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that the G-proposition does more than locate a causal relation: it ties G's intention to W1 and excludes rival sources, so it represents the actualisation as issuing from G's intention. I grant that. But the argument's requirement, as c005 and c006 state it, is that the outcome be represented as the agent's own activity rather than one among relevant alternatives. Your rejoinder asks what responsibility-relevant difference the further stance makes. The difference is this: a representation of W1's actualisation as G's intention-driven act, held by a cognizer who is G, is still a representation that G could hold while treating the act as an object of its knowledge rather than as its doing. Whether that gap matters is exactly the bridge premise, and the paper's c008 and c030 locate the requirement in agency-based attribution rather than in phenomenology. So I do not claim the gap is shown to matter independently. Here the argument is weakest: it needs robust responsibility to demand agent-relative representation, and the objection's question, which difference that makes, has not been answered by the argument as stated. I concede that c008 is not established by the 'own activity' phrasing alone. The premise the argument needs is: robust contrastive responsibility requires that the cognition represent the act under an agent-relative aspect that a rigid third-personal identifier cannot supply. Citing [W7203485685.c043] and [W7203485685.c027] for the claim that third-personal truths do not determine self-ascriptive content.

Revised premise: Robust contrastive responsibility requires that the agent's cognition represent the outcome under an agent-relative aspect (a stance of doing, not merely knowing) that a rigid third-personal identifier cannot supply.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
You show that “G actualised W1 because G intended W1” can identify, causally explain, and distinguish the unique actualiser with maximal third-personal precision. The argument need not deny that. Its claim is narrower: robust contrastive responsibility requires not merely a true explanation naming the source, but cognition in which the actualisation is represented as issuing from the agent’s own activity [W7203485685.c031]—a source-attribution requirement, not a claim about spatial or temporal self-location [W7203485685.c030].

But your case exposes a gap. If G’s rigid identifier is genuinely third-personal and yet G can form the relevant intention and exercise control through it, then the bare fact that the proposition is third-personal does not establish that it lacks agency-involving source representation. “G will actualise W1” might be a complete practical self-representation despite its grammar. The paper’s stronger thought is that third-personal truths do not by themselves determine the self-ascriptive content needed for robust responsibility [W7203485685.c027], not that no third-personal-looking cognition could play that role.

So c008, read as a claim about propositional form alone, does not survive your example. The conclusion can survive only if the relevant cognition is individuated by its role in intentional agency, not by whether it successfully identifies G.

Revised premise: For robust contrastive responsibility, the agent’s cognition must include a practically self-ascriptive mode of presentation under which the actualisation is represented as issuing from that very agent’s agency; third-personal source-identifying content alone does not guarantee this.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that Mira's display contains only impersonal propositions, and that she is contrastively responsible for the quarry outcome. But notice what c006 actually demands: cognition that represents the outcome as issuing from the agent's own activity rather than the alternative. Mira's cognition does contain an agent-involving element that the objection passes over: she represents which lever she is to pull as the one she intends, and she represents the village outcome as the one she is aiming at. That is a practical, intentional representation of her own selection, which the impersonal labels only describe. The question is whether this practical self-involvement is the de se content c006 requires, or merely a practical aid. [W7203485685.c007] claims self-ascriptive cognition is constitutive, not a mere aid, so the author must show that Mira's intention-directed deliberation is not replaceable by impersonal tracking. Here I think the objection has a real edge: Mira could in principle execute the whole selection with impersonal propositions plus a tag such as 'the pulling is mine' stored separately, which shows the first-personal element is an extra index rather than content about the outcome. The argument survives only if the author can show that the outcome-representation itself, not merely the act-representation, must be indexed to the agent. I cannot establish that from the case as given, and [W7203485685.c043] concedes that knowledge identifying the outcome does not by itself represent actualisation as issuing from one's agency. So I concede the premise as stated is vulnerable.

Revised premise: Robust contrastive responsibility requires cognition that represents the selected outcome, under the contrast with its alternative, as the result of an act the cognizing agent herself performs and intends, not merely as a state of the world tied to an impersonal lever-state.

rounds.speaker: defender_b
rounds.content:
Your Mira case shows that robust responsibility need not involve a display sentence such as “I am causing the quarry outcome.” But that is not the strongest reading of c006. Mira’s deliberation represents A and B as options she can select, and her intention-to-save-the-village is executed by pulling A; those contents locate the outcome in her agential alternative-set. The impersonal labels on the display therefore do not exhaust her cognition. If she merely observed that A opens gate 1 and that gate 1 sends water to the quarry, while lacking any cognition of A as her available act or of the outcome as attributable to her selection, the stipulated counterfactual and intentional control would not yet establish robust contrastive responsibility. The relevant demand is not linguistic first-person reference but cognition that explains why the quarry outcome is attributable to Mira rather than to B, the gate, or another operator [W7203485685.c044]. That is the Self-Location Constraint’s point: cognition must represent both the obtaining outcome and the subject as its source [W7203485685.c035]. Still, your example exposes an overstatement in c006: source-attribution need not be an explicit representation of the outcome “issuing from” the agent. The argument survives if c006 is read or revised to require an integrated agential representation of the relevant option and its outcome, rather than an occurrent self-ascription. This remains consistent with the author’s claim that self-ascriptive cognition is constitutive of robust agency attribution, not merely a finite-agent convenience [W7203485685.c007].

Revised premise: Robust contrastive responsibility requires cognition that represents the relevant outcome as attributable to the agent’s exercise of control among the relevant alternatives, though not necessarily by an explicit occurrent self-ascription.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that c005, as stated, fails. Ines represents the farmland flood under a contrast with the town flood, and she represents it as a foreseen consequence, not as her action. Your case shows that the requirement that the outcome be represented as the agent's own action is too strong. The argument's own supporting premises point to a weaker and more defensible requirement. c006 asks for cognition that represents an outcome as issuing from the agent's own activity rather than relevant alternatives [W7203485685.c006], and c044 asks for cognition that explains why the outcome is attributable to the agent rather than to alternatives [W7203485685.c044]. Both can be satisfied by Ines's cognition without the outcome being represented as her action. She represents her opening the spillway as her act, and represents the farmland flood as its result, under contrast with the town flood. Your point that the act and the outcome are different items is correct, and it is exactly why the premise should attach the agent-relative element to the act-outcome link, not to the outcome alone. The revised premise r2 does this. Whether it helps the divine case depends on whether God's cognition represents the act of actualising as his own, which is where the de se content is still needed. I therefore concede c005 as stated, and I defend the argument only with the replacement below.

Revised premise: Robust contrastive responsibility requires that the agent's cognition represent the selected outcome, under its contrast with the alternative, as the result of an act the agent herself performs and intends, rather than representing the outcome itself as her action.

rounds.speaker: defender_b

Your case shows that c005 is too strong if “the outcome” means the distal event itself. Ines need not represent the farmland’s flooding as identical with, or literally constituted by, her action of turning the wheel. She can represent it as a foreseen consequence and still be responsible for bringing it about rather than the town flood.

But this does not yet undermine the argument’s deeper source-attribution claim. Ines’s deliberation is not merely about an impersonal hydrographic fact: she represents flooding the farmland rather than the town as what will issue from her selected intervention. The relevant agent-relative content can attach to the act–outcome relation: “by doing this, I bring about that,” rather than to a description that redescribes the flooding itself as an action. That is the kind of cognition that explains why the result is attributable to her rather than to the relevant alternative source or course of events [W7203485685.c044], and it preserves the contrastive source condition [W7203485685.c006].

So the intended route to the divine conclusion survives, but not through c005 as written. A rigid third-personal description of an actualised world may identify the result without supplying the first-personal stance of selecting it as one’s own act; that remains the pressure behind the de se conclusion [W7203485685.c008; W7203485685.c009].

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that the bare inference from robust responsibility to de se content needs support, and the argument's own history shows it: the unstated mp premise was replaced by r1 and r2 after earlier trials. But your engineer case does not reach the revised premise. Your engineer's content, 'the agent with goodness G selects W1 over W0 because G favours W1,' is a third-personal explanation of selection by a value. It tracks counterfactual dependence on G, which is why you can say her responsibility is robust. The argument's claim, however, is that contrastive responsibility requires cognition representing the outcome as the result of an act the agent herself performs and intends [W7203485685.arg1.r2], and [W7203485685.c006] ties this to attribution as issuing from the agent's own activity rather than from relevant alternatives. An indexed value-state can ground counterfactual sensitivity without representing an act of selecting as one's own. So the engineer shows that counterfactual sensitivity to values suffices for one notion of source-tracking, not that it suffices for the act-intention notion the argument needs. Your case thus leaves r2 untouched, though it does show that the mp premise, stated without r2, overreaches. I also note that [W7203485685.c008] already grants that a third-personal proposition does not itself represent actualisation under the first-personal aspect, so the disagreement is over whether act-intention is required, not over the bare contrast. I think the argument survives in its r2 form. Whether r2 is independently motivated, rather than just stipulated to fit the conclusion, is the real pressure point, and I concede that the mp version as written does not survive.

Your engineer case establishes an important limit: causal dependence on the engineer's values, even counterfactual dependence, does not by itself show that her cognition represents W1 as her act rather than as the selection of whoever instantiates G. The description may be read externally: it identifies a value-bearing agent and a selection, without locating the cognizer as that agent. That is precisely the gap between a causal/attributive relation and an adequate contrastive agency explanation [W7203485685.c046].

If, however, you stipulate that the engineer's value-indexed representation is genuinely action-guiding for her—she selects W1 under the representation that this is the act she performs for these reasons—then it is no longer merely impersonal lever-state content. It has the agent-relative stance at issue in the revised premise: cognition represents W1, against W0, as resulting from an act the cognizer performs and intends. The paper's claim is that this action-guiding role is not exhausted by third-personal representation [W7203485685.c042], and that robust responsibility requires representing the outcome as issuing from the agent's own activity rather than alternatives [W7203485685.c006].

Still, the original premise overstates what follows from responsibility alone. The argument survives only if the proposed third-personal structure cannot supply that agent-relative, action-guiding stance without de se content.

rounds.content: Not a misreading: The objection directly attacks the unstated premise as stated by denying that representing God as the source requires irreducible de se content and proposing uniquely identifying third-personal content as sufficient. It therefore does not attribute a different premise or conclusion to the argument.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content: You are right that the argument needs more than the bare fact that God controls the outcome; control is a matter of who does the actualising, and a fully informed third-personal description can capture that. But the argument's premise, in its revised forms (r1 to r4), is about how the outcome is represented in the cognition of the one contrastively responsible, not about who controls it. The claim is that the selected outcome must be represented under its contrast with the alternative as the result of an act the agent herself performs and intends. Your God knows 'God alone intentionally actualises W1' and 'God could instead actualise W0', but these are propositions about God, and a rigid identifier 'God' supplies the referent without supplying the agent-relative stance of doing. Knowing that a certain agent performs an act is not yet representing that act as one's own performance, and the self-ascriptive gap is what [W7203485685.c008] and [W7203485685.c027] identify. Your objection thus reduces the source-representation requirement to control plus a true identity judgement, which is the move [W7203485685.c040] offers and which the argument must reject: 'I am God' is itself a de se thought that the third-personal description does not contain. The objection's own phrase 'changes only how the source is represented' concedes the point at issue, since the argument's requirement is precisely about how the source is represented. I do not claim divine cognition must be indexical in the way human perception is; [W7204221334.a1] and [W4220715675.a2] remind us that causal and epistemic access to God's agency is a separate matter, and I do not rely on it here.

rounds.speaker: attacker
rounds.content: You restate the disputed requirement without defending it. I concede that the mode of representation differs, not that responsibility depends on that difference. The third-personal cognition already represents the relevant contrast, intentional act, causal source, alternatives, and reason-responsive control. Calling these propositions “about God” does not show that they fail to guide God’s choice or constitute God’s intention. Nor does my case require the further judgment “I am God”: the uniquely identified agent who deliberates, intends, and acts is numerically the cognizer, whether or not that identity is represented de se. To defeat the objection, you must explain why robust responsibility requires self-ascriptive presentation in addition to accurate representation of one’s intentional control. Appealing to an “agent-relative stance of doing” merely renames that unestablished necessity.

rounds.speaker: defender_a
rounds.content:
You are right that the argument's requirement is about representation, not control, and I accept that the revised premises r1 to r4 are what is at stake. Your rejoinder asks me to show why robust responsibility requires self-ascriptive presentation over and above accurate representation of one's intentional control. I cannot show that from the materials available. The argument's support for the requirement rests on [W7203485685.c008] and [W7203485685.c027], which claim that third-personal truths do not determine the self-ascriptive content needed for contrastive responsibility, but those are premises the argument asserts rather than establishes. Your case that the uniquely identified deliberating agent is numerically the cognizer, without any further first-personal judgement, is a serious alternative: it makes the requirement one of accurate self-identity under a rigid description, which the argument has not shown to be insufficient. The phrase 'stance of doing' does, as you say, rename the necessity rather than supply it. I therefore concede that the argument as stated does not survive this objection. The argument would need a premise that the agent's responsibility for an outcome is robust only if the agent's cognition contains an irreducible de se mode of presenting herself as the performer of the act, with a supporting argument that rigid third-personal identification of an agent who intends and controls the outcome cannot secure that mode. Divine foreknowledge and epistemic access to God's agency, as in [W7204221334.a1] and [W4220715675.a2], do not bear on this and I do not rely on them.

Revised premise: Robust contrastive responsibility requires that the agent's cognition contain an irreducible de se mode of presenting herself as the performer of the selected act, which no rigid third-personal identification of an intentionally controlling agent can supply.

rounds.content:
You are right that the stipulated third-personal truths can identify God uniquely, describe God’s intentional control, and explain why W1 obtains rather than W0. The argument need not deny any of that. Nor does it infer a defect in causal control merely from the absence of a first-personal mode of presentation.

It requires cognition of the W1/W0 contrast as settled by an act the cognizing agent performs and intends. A proposition such as “God alone intentionally actualises W1” represents a fact about God’s agency; it does not yet constitute God’s self-ascription of that agency. That is precisely the distinction the paper marks: third-personal content identifies the outcome and its source without representing actualisation as issuing from the subject’s own agency [W7203485685.c043], and it does not determine the required self-ascriptive content [W7203485685.c027].

Still, your case exposes an unsupported bridge in arg1.mp: why must this agent-relative practical representation be irreducibly de se, rather than a complete third-personal representation possessed by the sole divine agent? The argument survives only if that bridge is made explicit; uniqueness and causal completeness alone do not establish it.

objection.text: Consider a long-running coastal engineer, Mara, who sets a sea wall's height by a stored model of tides. Her cognition does not represent herself as 'the source' of the wall's height; it represents the wall at 4 metres as the output of a calculation that fixes the tide threshold, and she can say which alternative heights she rejected and why. Suppose the town later asks who is responsible for the wall being 4 metres rather than 3. Mara is robustly contrastively responsible: had she chosen 3, the flood would have come, and her choice is the difference-maker. Yet her cognition contains no first-personal marker that the height issues from her agency. It contains the content 'the wall is 4 m because the threshold is 4 m,' with her choice modelled as one causal node among others. Her responsibility is secured by counterfactual dependence and by the structure of her deliberation over relevant alternatives, not by any self-representation of the outcome as her own. The same structure can hold for an agent whose cognition is wholly third-personal about the outcome while representing its contrastive alternatives explicitly.
objection.premise_fails_because: Premise c031 fails because it requires divine cognition to represent God as the source of W1 rather than W0, yet Mara's case shows robust contrastive responsibility can be secured by cognition that represents the outcome and its rejected alternatives without any source-representing, first-personal content.

objection.text: Ines, a reservoir controller, faces rising water during a storm. Opening the east spillway will flood farmland; doing nothing will let the dam overtop and flood the town. She studies hydrographs, weighs crop losses against lives, and concludes, in exactly these terms, 'The farmland should flood rather than the town.' She opens the spillway and the farmland floods. The inquiry finds her robustly responsible for the farmland flooding rather than the town: she foresaw it, compared it with the alternative, chose it knowingly, and could have done otherwise. Yet the outcome she represented, the farmland under water, was never represented as her action. It is a hydrological event downstream, and she represented it as one. The only thing she represented as her doing was turning the spillway wheel, and that is a different item from the outcome for which she is held responsible. Her responsibility for the flood rests on representing the flood as a foreseen consequence she was choosing between, not on representing the flood as her action.
objection.premise_fails_because: W7203485685.c005 fails because Ines is robustly responsible for the farmland flooding rather than the town while her cognition represents that outcome only as a foreseen consequence she chose, not as her own action.

objection.text: A control-room operator, Mira, selects lever A after reviewing two labeled simulations: A will divert a flood into an empty quarry; B will divert it into a village. She intends to save the village and pulls A. Her display represents only impersonal propositions: “A opens gate 1,” “gate 1 sends water to quarry,” and “B sends water to village.” It never represents the flood outcome as issuing from Mira’s own activity; it tracks lever states and consequences. The gate opens, the flood reaches the quarry, and the village is saved. Mira is robustly contrastively responsible for the quarry outcome rather than the village outcome: she knew the alternatives, deliberately selected the difference-making option, and would have pulled B had she intended the village outcome. Yet her cognition need not represent the outcome as issuing from her own activity rather than the alternative.
objection.premise_fails_because: W7203485685.c006 fails because robust contrastive responsibility can arise from deliberate, informed selection among alternatives even when cognition represents only impersonal causal relations.

objection.text: God’s cognition uses only a rigid identifier, “G,” for the unique being whose intentions directly control which world becomes actual. G considers W0 and W1, judges W1 better, forms the intention expressed as “G will actualise W1,” and W1 consequently becomes actual. G then knows the proposition “G actualised W1 rather than W0 because G intended W1.” The identifier is third-personal: it carries no first-personal mode of presentation. Yet the proposition identifies the source perfectly. It singles out the unique controller, connects that being’s intention to the resulting world, and excludes every alternative source. Nothing further supplied by “I actualised W1” would improve the attribution of the actualisation to G.
objection.premise_fails_because: W7203485685.c008 fails because a third-personal proposition can identify God’s intention and controlling activity as the source of actualisation without representing them under a first-personal aspect.

objection.text: Consider a divine cognition that represents the proposition 'God actualises W1' and, in addition, represents W1 as preferred over W0 by a standard it itself instantiates, with no de se indexical content. Call it a purely third-personal but evaluatively structured representation. Now suppose a second agent, an idealised engineer modelled on this God, whose cognition likewise contains the indexical-free content 'the agent with goodness G selects W1 over W0 because G favours W1.' The engineer is robustly and contrastively responsible for selecting W1 rather than W0: the selection flows from her own values, would have differed had her values differed, and no alternative source intervenes. Yet her cognition contains no first-personal 'I am the source' representation. The premise assumes that robust contrastive responsibility requires self-representation as source, but the case shows that source-tracking can be carried by a counterfactually sensitive, value-indexed structure that the agent's own cognition encodes without irreducible de se content. The inference from robust responsibility to irreducible de se content therefore lacks support.
objection.premise_fails_because: The premise wrongly assumes that representing God as source of W1 over W0 requires irreducible de se content, when counterfactually sensitive, value-indexed third-personal representation can secure robust contrastive source-attribution without it.

objection.text: God creates an initial state containing two free creatures, Ada and Ben. Whether Ada will later betray Ben is genuinely unsettled. Nothing in God's decree, nature, or knowledge fixes it, because no fact about it exists yet. Let W1 be the history where Ada betrays and W0 the history where she stays loyal. They share every divine act and differ only in Ada's choice. God is robustly responsible for creating this risky, open arrangement rather than a closed or empty one. God weighed the stakes, knew betrayal was possible, and accepted that risk for the sake of real love. Yet divine cognition cannot represent God as the source of W1 rather than W0. At creation there is no settled W1 to represent, and once Ada chooses, she is the source of that contrast, not God. God's robust responsibility attaches to the contrast between opening this field of possibilities and not opening it. It does not attach to the complete-world contrast, so it never needs the representation c031 demands.
objection.premise_fails_because: W7203485685.c031 fails because in an open future God is robustly responsible for creating an unsettled world without being, or representing himself as, the source of one complete world rather than another.

objection.text: Molinism holds that God knows, before creating, every true counterfactual of creaturely freedom. God knows that if placed in circumstances C, Mara would freely help, while if placed in D, she would freely refuse. God considers W1, containing C, and W0, containing D, under complete third-personal descriptions: in W1 Mara helps; in W0 Mara refuses. God chooses to actualise W1 because its freely chosen goods are preferable. The choice is robustly contrastive: God could actualise W0, knows exactly its consequences, and intentionally actualises W1 instead. Yet the source attribution needed is exhausted by the true proposition that God actualises W1 rather than W0; no irreducible first-personal content is required. Divine responsibility arises from intentional selection among feasible worlds informed by middle knowledge, not from a de se mode of presentation.
objection.premise_fails_because: W7203485685.arg1.mp fails because Molinist divine responsibility for selecting W1 over W0 can rest on complete third-personal middle knowledge and intentional choice without irreducible de se content.

objection.text: Suppose God knows the third-personal truths that God alone intentionally actualises W1, that God could instead actualise W0, and that W1 occurs because of God’s fully informed, reason-responsive choice. God also has complete knowledge of every relevant alternative and causal dependency, but divine cognition contains no irreducible first-personal content. Nothing here prevents the choice from issuing from God, being controlled by God, or appropriately reflecting God’s reasons; omitting a distinct first-personal mode of presentation changes only how the source is represented, not who controls the outcome. Thus W7203485685.arg1.mp fails because source attribution can be fully represented by uniquely identifying third-personal content without irreducible de se content.
objection.premise_fails_because: Uniquely identifying third-personal cognition can attribute the actualisation to God as its controlled, intentional source without irreducible de se content.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content: The objection's G-proposition does pick out the unique controller and its intention, and I grant that it excludes rival sources. But the argument's demand, stated in c005 and c006, is not exclusion of other sources; it is that the cognition represent the outcome as issuing from the agent's own activity rather than from relevant alternatives. 'G actualised W1 rather than W0 because G intended W1' represents G as one bearer of a causal relation, which G can know without being in any position to take that relation as its own doing. The objection's own gloss, that the identifier 'carries no first-personal mode of presentation,' concedes the point at issue: the disputed content is precisely the mode of presentation. Note also that c030 holds the Self-Location Constraint concerns agency-based source attribution, not spatiotemporal presence, so the objection's appeal to a perfect identification is not yet an appeal to the right kind of attribution. A rigid designator fixes reference; it does not by itself fix the agent's stance toward the act. I would still press the objector to say why a third-personal representation of one's own intention and its effect should count as representing that effect as one's own action, since that is where the dispute now lies. The argument's bridge premise, that robust responsibility requires such agent-relative representation, remains the load-bearing and contestable step, and I would not claim the c008 rejoinder settles it.

turn.speaker: attacker
turn.content: You distinguish identifying the agent from representing the act as “its own,” but you have not shown that the latter requires a first-personal mode of presentation. The G-proposition already represents the actualisation as issuing from G’s intention and activity, not merely as a causal relation borne by G. Since G is the cognizer, the proposition concerns the cognizer’s own intention and action even if it does not present them under “I.” Saying that G could know this without “taking” it as its own doing simply restates the disputed requirement. What responsibility-relevant difference would that further stance make? The representation already tracks who controlled the alternatives, which intention selected W1, and whose activity produced it. Unless robust responsibility depends on a special phenomenology or practical role available only to first-personal content, your appeal to “own activity” cannot establish c008; it merely builds irreducible de se representation into that phrase.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content:
You are right that the G-proposition does more than locate a causal relation: it ties G's intention to W1 and excludes rival sources, so it represents the actualisation as issuing from G's intention. I grant that. But the argument's requirement, as c005 and c006 state it, is that the outcome be represented as the agent's own activity rather than one among relevant alternatives. Your rejoinder asks what responsibility-relevant difference the further stance makes. The difference is this: a representation of W1's actualisation as G's intention-driven act, held by a cognizer who is G, is still a representation that G could hold while treating the act as an object of its knowledge rather than as its doing. Whether that gap matters is exactly the bridge premise, and the paper's c008 and c030 locate the requirement in agency-based attribution rather than in phenomenology. So I do not claim the gap is shown to matter independently. Here the argument is weakest: it needs robust responsibility to demand agent-relative representation, and the objection's question, which difference that makes, has not been answered by the argument as stated. I concede that c008 is not established by the 'own activity' phrasing alone. The premise the argument needs is: robust contrastive responsibility requires that the cognition represent the act under an agent-relative aspect that a rigid third-personal identifier cannot supply. Citing [W7203485685.c043] and [W7203485685.c027] for the claim that third-personal truths do not determine self-ascriptive content.

Revised premise: Robust contrastive responsibility requires that the agent's cognition represent the outcome under an agent-relative aspect (a stance of doing, not merely knowing) that a rigid third-personal identifier cannot supply.
turn.revised_premise: Robust contrastive responsibility requires that the agent's cognition represent the outcome under an agent-relative aspect (a stance of doing, not merely knowing) that a rigid third-personal identifier cannot supply.

turn.speaker: defender_b
turn.content:
You show that “G actualised W1 because G intended W1” can identify, causally explain, and distinguish the unique actualiser with maximal third-personal precision. The argument need not deny that. Its claim is narrower: robust contrastive responsibility requires not merely a true explanation naming the source, but cognition in which the actualisation is represented as issuing from the agent’s own activity [W7203485685.c031]—a source-attribution requirement, not a claim about spatial or temporal self-location [W7203485685.c030].

But your case exposes a gap. If G’s rigid identifier is genuinely third-personal and yet G can form the relevant intention and exercise control through it, then the bare fact that the proposition is third-personal does not establish that it lacks agency-involving source representation. “G will actualise W1” might be a complete practical self-representation despite its grammar. The paper’s stronger thought is that third-personal truths do not by themselves determine the self-ascriptive content needed for robust responsibility [W7203485685.c027], not that no third-personal-looking cognition could play that role.

So c008, read as a claim about propositional form alone, does not survive your example. The conclusion can survive only if the relevant cognition is individuated by its role in intentional agency, not by whether it successfully identifies G.

Revised premise: For robust contrastive responsibility, the agent’s cognition must include a practically self-ascriptive mode of presentation under which the actualisation is represented as issuing from that very agent’s agency; third-personal source-identifying content alone does not guarantee this.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content:
You are right that Mira's display contains only impersonal propositions, and that she is contrastively responsible for the quarry outcome. But notice what c006 actually demands: cognition that represents the outcome as issuing from the agent's own activity rather than the alternative. Mira's cognition does contain an agent-involving element that the objection passes over: she represents which lever she is to pull as the one she intends, and she represents the village outcome as the one she is aiming at. That is a practical, intentional representation of her own selection, which the impersonal labels only describe. The question is whether this practical self-involvement is the de se content c006 requires, or merely a practical aid. [W7203485685.c007] claims self-ascriptive cognition is constitutive, not a mere aid, so the author must show that Mira's intention-directed deliberation is not replaceable by impersonal tracking. Here I think the objection has a real edge: Mira could in principle execute the whole selection with impersonal propositions plus a tag such as 'the pulling is mine' stored separately, which shows the first-personal element is an extra index rather than content about the outcome. The argument survives only if the author can show that the outcome-representation itself, not merely the act-representation, must be indexed to the agent. I cannot establish that from the case as given, and [W7203485685.c043] concedes that knowledge identifying the outcome does not by itself represent actualisation as issuing from one's agency. So I concede the premise as stated is vulnerable.

Revised premise: Robust contrastive responsibility requires cognition that represents the selected outcome, under the contrast with its alternative, as the result of an act the cognizing agent herself performs and intends, not merely as a state of the world tied to an impersonal lever-state.

turn.speaker: defender_b
turn.content:
Your Mira case shows that robust responsibility need not involve a display sentence such as “I am causing the quarry outcome.” But that is not the strongest reading of c006. Mira’s deliberation represents A and B as options she can select, and her intention-to-save-the-village is executed by pulling A; those contents locate the outcome in her agential alternative-set. The impersonal labels on the display therefore do not exhaust her cognition. If she merely observed that A opens gate 1 and that gate 1 sends water to the quarry, while lacking any cognition of A as her available act or of the outcome as attributable to her selection, the stipulated counterfactual and intentional control would not yet establish robust contrastive responsibility. The relevant demand is not linguistic first-person reference but cognition that explains why the quarry outcome is attributable to Mira rather than to B, the gate, or another operator [W7203485685.c044]. That is the Self-Location Constraint’s point: cognition must represent both the obtaining outcome and the subject as its source [W7203485685.c035]. Still, your example exposes an overstatement in c006: source-attribution need not be an explicit representation of the outcome “issuing from” the agent. The argument survives if c006 is read or revised to require an integrated agential representation of the relevant option and its outcome, rather than an occurrent self-ascription. This remains consistent with the author’s claim that self-ascriptive cognition is constitutive of robust agency attribution, not merely a finite-agent convenience [W7203485685.c007].

Revised premise: Robust contrastive responsibility requires cognition that represents the relevant outcome as attributable to the agent’s exercise of control among the relevant alternatives, though not necessarily by an explicit occurrent self-ascription.

objection.text: Consider a water-main control room. Engineer Ada holds a valve-state map: valve V open routes flow to district A, closed routes it to district B. She has no first-personal intention to 'do' this; her supervisor has ordered the switch, and a timer she set earlier fires automatically. Yet she knows exactly which outcome is hers under the contrast: she is the one who wired the timer and the flow goes to A because of her configuration. Her cognition represents the outcome contrastively as the result of the configured state she set up, not as an act she performs and intends at the moment of flow. Her responsibility for routing to A rather than B is robust: had she set the timer differently, the flow would have gone to B, and she would be blamed and credited accordingly. Her cognition contains no irreducible de se act-representation of the switching; it contains a third-personal state-description tied to her earlier decision. So robust contrastive responsibility does not require the agent's cognition to represent the selected outcome as the result of an act she herself performs and intends, in the present, under the contrast.

turn.content:
You are right that c005, as stated, fails. Ines represents the farmland flood under a contrast with the town flood, and she represents it as a foreseen consequence, not as her action. Your case shows that the requirement that the outcome be represented as the agent's own action is too strong. The argument's own supporting premises point to a weaker and more defensible requirement. c006 asks for cognition that represents an outcome as issuing from the agent's own activity rather than relevant alternatives [W7203485685.c006], and c044 asks for cognition that explains why the outcome is attributable to the agent rather than to alternatives [W7203485685.c044]. She represents her opening the spillway as her act, and represents the farmland flood as its result, under contrast with the town flood. The revised premise r2 does this. Whether it helps the divine case depends on whether God's cognition represents the act of actualising as his own, which is where the de se content is still needed. I therefore concede c005 as stated, and I defend the argument only with the replacement below.
