turn.content:
Your case shows that c005 is too strong if “the outcome” means the distal event itself. Ines need not represent the farmland’s flooding as identical with, or literally constituted by, her action of turning the wheel. She can represent it as a foreseen consequence and still be responsible for bringing it about rather than the town flood.

But this does not yet undermine the argument’s deeper source-attribution claim. Ines’s deliberation is not merely about an impersonal hydrographic fact: she represents flooding the farmland rather than the town as what will issue from her selected intervention. The relevant agent-relative content can attach to the act–outcome relation: “by doing this, I bring about that,” rather than to a description that redescribes the flooding itself as an action. That is the kind of cognition that explains why the result is attributable to her rather than to the relevant alternative source or course of events [W7203485685.c044], and it preserves the contrastive source condition [W7203485685.c006].

So the intended route to the divine conclusion survives, but not through c005 as written. A rigid third-personal description of an actualised world may identify the result without supplying the first-personal stance of selecting it as one’s own act; that remains the pressure behind the de se conclusion [W7203485685.c008; W7203485685.c009].

The paper's claim is that this action-guiding role is not exhausted by third-personal representation [W7203485685.c042], and that robust responsibility requires representing the outcome as issuing from the agent's own activity rather than alternatives [W7203485685.c006].

objection.text: Consider Ada, a town clerk who must allot a single grant to either Riverside or Hillcrest. She reasons: 'Riverside has the better case, so the grant goes to Riverside.' Her cognition represents the outcome, Riverside funded, under its contrast with Hillcrest funded, and she intends it. Yet nothing in her thought represents the funding as the product of an act she herself performs. The content 'Riverside is funded because of the ranking' is entirely third-personal, and her responsibility for the allocation is nonetheless robust: had she ranked Hillcrest higher, Hillcrest would have been funded, and she would be blamed for either choice. Her cognition is intentionally directed at the contrast and at the outcome, with no first-personal self-representation as agent. So representing the selected outcome under its contrast, as the result of an intended act, is satisfiable without representing the outcome as one's own act. The premise demands an extra first-personal layer that the case shows is not needed for contrastive, robust responsibility.
objection.premise_fails_because: The premise requires that cognition represent the outcome as the result of an act the agent performs and intends, but Ada's robust contrastive responsibility is secured by intended, contrast-sensitive representation of the outcome itself, with no first-personal representation of herself as the performer of that act.

objection.text: Consider a water-network engineer, Ruth, who must choose between two valve configurations, C1 and C0, to route flow to a district. She sets the valves to C1 by following a procedure card that her team's software generated from a value-indexed table: 'if reservoir level ≥ 40m, use C1 for equal pressure.' She intends the outcome of equal pressure, and she knows her act is the one that produces C1, yet her cognition represents the outcome only as tied to the table entry, never as 'the result of my act.' Suppose she reliably produces C1 rather than C0 and is therefore the robustly responsible source of the contrast. Her cognition contains no first-personal representation of the selected outcome as her own performed act; it represents the configuration through the value-indexed structure. Yet her contrastive responsibility is robust. So a state tied to a value-indexed structure, without an agent-indexed act-representation, can ground robust contrastive responsibility.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content: You are right that the argument needs more than the bare fact that God controls the outcome; control is a matter of who does the actualising, and a fully informed third-personal description can capture that. But the argument's premise, in its revised forms (r1 to r4), is about how the outcome is represented in the cognition of the one contrastively responsible, not about who controls it. The claim is that the selected outcome must be represented under its contrast with the alternative as the result of an act the agent herself performs and intends. Your God knows 'God alone intentionally actualises W1' and 'God could instead actualise W0', but these are propositions about God, and a rigid identifier 'God' supplies the referent without supplying the agent-relative stance of doing. Knowing that a certain agent performs an act is not yet representing that act as one's own performance, and the self-ascriptive gap is what [W7203485685.c008] and [W7203485685.c027] identify. Your objection thus reduces the source-representation requirement to control plus a true identity judgement, which is the move [W7203485685.c040] offers and which the argument must reject: 'I am God' is itself a de se thought that the third-personal description does not contain. The objection's own phrase 'changes only how the source is represented' concedes the point at issue, since the argument's requirement is precisely about how the source is represented. I do not claim divine cognition must be indexical in the way human perception is; [W7204221334.a1] and [W4220715675.a2] remind us that causal and epistemic access to God's agency is a separate matter, and I do not rely on it here.

turn.speaker: attacker
turn.content: You restate the disputed requirement without defending it. I concede that the mode of representation differs, not that responsibility depends on that difference. The third-personal cognition already represents the relevant contrast, intentional act, causal source, alternatives, and reason-responsive control. Calling these propositions “about God” does not show that they fail to guide God’s choice or constitute God’s intention. Nor does my case require the further judgment “I am God”: the uniquely identified agent who deliberates, intends, and acts is numerically the cognizer, whether or not that identity is represented de se. To defeat the objection, you must explain why robust responsibility requires self-ascriptive presentation in addition to accurate representation of one’s intentional control. Appealing to an “agent-relative stance of doing” merely renames that unestablished necessity.

turn.speaker: defender_a
turn.content:
You are right that the argument's requirement is about representation, not control, and I accept that the revised premises r1 to r4 are what is at stake. Your rejoinder asks me to show why robust responsibility requires self-ascriptive presentation over and above accurate representation of one's intentional control. I cannot show that from the materials available. The argument's support for the requirement rests on [W7203485685.c008] and [W7203485685.c027], which claim that third-personal truths do not determine the self-ascriptive content needed for contrastive responsibility, but those are premises the argument asserts rather than establishes. Your case that the uniquely identified deliberating agent is numerically the cognizer, without any further first-personal judgement, is a serious alternative: it makes the requirement one of accurate self-identity under a rigid description, which the argument has not shown to be insufficient. The phrase 'stance of doing' does, as you say, rename the necessity rather than supply it. I therefore concede that the argument as stated does not survive this objection. The argument would need a premise that the agent's responsibility for an outcome is robust only if the agent's cognition contains an irreducible de se mode of presenting herself as the performer of the act, with a supporting argument that rigid third-personal identification of an agent who intends and controls the outcome cannot secure that mode. Divine foreknowledge and epistemic access to God's agency, as in [W7204221334.a1] and [W4220715675.a2], do not bear on this and I do not rely on them.

Revised premise: Robust contrastive responsibility requires that the agent's cognition contain an irreducible de se mode of presenting herself as the performer of the selected act, which no rigid third-personal identification of an intentionally controlling agent can supply.

turn.speaker: defender_b
turn.content:
You are right that the stipulated third-personal truths can identify God uniquely, describe God’s intentional control, and explain why W1 obtains rather than W0. The argument need not deny any of that. Nor does it infer a defect in causal control merely from the absence of a first-personal mode of presentation.

But robust contrastive responsibility is stronger than being the uniquely described cause of a reason-responsive event. It requires cognition of the W1/W0 contrast as settled by an act the cognizing agent performs and intends. A proposition such as “God alone intentionally actualises W1” represents a fact about God’s agency; it does not yet constitute God’s self-ascription of that agency. That is precisely the distinction the paper marks: third-personal content identifies the outcome and its source without representing actualisation as issuing from the subject’s own agency [W7203485685.c043], and it does not determine the required self-ascriptive content [W7203485685.c027].

Still, your case exposes an unsupported bridge in arg1.mp: why must this agent-relative practical representation be irreducibly de se, rather than a complete third-personal representation possessed by the sole divine agent? The argument survives only if that bridge is made explicit; uniqueness and causal completeness alone do not establish it.
